title: What 20 years of US data say
data: Daily closes Jan 2007 – Oct 2026, 2,672 US stocks listed today, 199,041 first breakouts from bases of 25+ days with $1M+ daily dollar volume and a full year of data after. Returns are 1-year excess over the S&P 500 from the breakout close; 'Failed' = closed 5%+ back inside the base within 20 sessions; 'Doubled' = rose 100%+ at some point within the year.
caveats: Only stocks still listed today (companies that were delisted or acquired are missing, which flatters all returns a little, but affects every bucket). Averages are trimmed at the 0.5% tails. Past results are evidence, not a promise.
findings: In US stocks a longer base did NOT lead to a bigger move — the opposite of the Indian result. Among breakouts in an uptrend (above a rising 150-day and the 200-day average) with RS 70+, 50–99-day bases beat the S&P 500 by about 4% over the next year and 25–49-day bases by about 2%, while 200–399-day bases lagged by about 1%, 400–799-day bases by about 3% and 800+ day bases by about 6%. The same order held in 2007–16 and in 2017–26 (checked on breakouts with RS 80+ in an uptrend: 50–99 days best, 800+ days worst in both halves).

Long bases were steadier rather than stronger: fewer of their breakouts failed (about 27–31% for 400+ days against 37% for 25–49 days), but far fewer of them doubled within the year (2–4% against 8%).

RS at the breakout was the factor that mattered most in the last decade: in 2017–26, breakouts with RS 90+ beat the S&P 500 by about 8.5% a year, against −1.7% for RS under 50 and −2.2% for RS 70–79. In 2007–16 the RS bands were close together (+2% to +3%). RS 90+ breakouts also failed more often (about 41–45%), so they need tight stops.

The Base Score, built and tested on NSE data, did not sort US returns: its bands averaged between −0.7% and +1.3% a year over the S&P 500, and in 2017–26 the 80+ band lagged (−3.6%). It did cut failed breakouts from 39% (under 40) to 30% (70+). On US stocks read it as a reliability gauge (fewer failed breakouts), not a return forecast; RS and the 50–199-day base length carry the return edge.

Context: from 2017 to 2026 a few giant companies carried the cap-weighted S&P 500, so the median stock lagged it — most buckets have negative medians. Compare the buckets with each other, not with zero.
